title.en: Of the Supreme Being: Aiounun Kondi, Dweller in the Height
title.zh: 至高神艾奧蒙孔迪：高居者

region.zh: 圭亞那濱海阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part I 'Legends of the Arawaks', 'Of the Supreme Being'

summary.en: There is a mighty One above, and like Him there is none: He sits on high, above the sky, where none can see His throne. He was there ere He made the world, with stars, and moon, and sun, and evermore He will be there. The Arawak tongue gives Him no proper name but titles more than one: 'Dweller in the Height' — Aiounun Kondi — since there He sits alone; the 'Great Our Father', though to Him for comfort none have gone; and 'Our Maker', Wamurreti-kwonci, of whom they oft speak but never call upon. Calm He sits above the sky; to Him for succour none can fly, He is so high above.
summary.zh: 至高者獨一無二；居於天上天，人莫見其座。造日月星辰與世界之先，彼已在；萬物運行之終，彼仍在。土語無其本名，惟多尊號：曰『高居者』艾奧蒙孔迪，以獨坐於高也；曰『大父』，然未嘗有求告者；曰『造者』瓦穆瑞提孔迪，常言之而不祈也。彼靜居高天，人莫能仰求——蓋其太高矣。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett in 1880 and versified by him; read critically — the hymnic form and titles are filtered through missionary interpretation, and im Thurn warned that such 'Supreme Being' passages may be colonial reflections.

passages.text: There is a mighty One above: and like Him there is none! He sits on high, above the sky, where none can see His throne. He was there ere He made the world, with stars, and moon, and sun; and evermore He will be there, when each its course has run.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Of the Supreme Being'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Our tongue gives Him no proper name, but titles more than one: we call Him 'Dweller in the Height' — Aiounun Kondi — since there He sits alone; the 'Great Our Father', though to Him for comfort none have gone; and 'Our Maker' — Wamurreti-kwonci — of whom we oft speak, but never call upon. That Mighty Maker all things formed; 'tis He that made them move; and food for all things He bestows, which seems a proof of love. But calm He sits above the sky: to Him for succour none can fly — He is so high above!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Of the Supreme Being'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Komaka Throne: Creation from the Silk-Cotton Tree
title.zh: 柯瑪卡座：木棉樹上之創造

region.zh: 圭亞那濱海阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part I 'Legends of the Arawaks', 'Origin of Living Creatures'

summary.en: Old men told, beneath the sacred tree, how moon and sun, earth and sky, and wide-spread sea lay before the Mighty One. Still no life was in the land; nothing then was seen to move. Then His seat, the Komaka — the wondrous silk-cotton tree whose branches were mid the clouds, with earth and sea far below — He caused to grow. From that bright-green throne His hand scattered twigs and bark around: some in air, and some on land, some the sparkling waters found. Soon He saw with life abound water, air, and solid ground: shining fishes darted where the woody fragments fell; others sported through the air; beasts and reptiles moved on solid ground; and men and women stood upright, raised by their great Maker's hand. Wild fruits first were human food, and water man's sole drink; no bold hunters roamed the wood, none would take life away — beasts and birds would sport and play with young children day by day, until Wadili came, took the maidens for his wives, and taught hunting, fishing, and husbandry.
summary.zh: 老人們於神樹之下言：日月、天地、浩海初陳於至高者之前，而大地無生，萬物不動。乃令其座——神柯瑪卡木棉樹——生焉，枝在雲端，地海在下。自翠座之上，其手散枝皮於四方：入空者化鳥，入水者化魚，落地者化獸、化蟲、化男女——直立者，造物主之手所舉也。初民食野果，飲白水；無獵者，無殺生；鳥獸與孩童日日嬉戲。後瓦迪利至，娶其女，教以漁獵農耕之術。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880 in metrical form; paraphrased into prose and read critically.

passages.text: Here, beneath this sacred tree, old men told how moon and sun, earth and sky, and wide-spread sea lay before the Mighty One. Waves soft murmuring beat the strand, gentle breezes sighed above — still no life was in the land, no sweet birds sang songs of love; o'er the plain and through the grove nothing then was seen to move. Then His seat, the Komaka — the wondrous silk-cotton tree — He caused to grow: 'midst the clouds its branches were, earth and sea lay far below.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Origin of Living Creatures'; not verbatim.

passages.text: From that bright-green throne His hand scattered twigs and bark around: some in air, and some on land; some the sparkling waters found. Soon He saw with life abound water, air, and solid ground! Those which fell upon the stream found a pleasant shelter there — shining fishes dart and gleam where those woody fragments were; others sported through the air, bright with wings and feathers fair; moving on solid ground beasts and reptiles then were found, spreading thence to fill the land. Men and women upright stand, raised by their great Maker's hand.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Origin of Living Creatures'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Wild fruits first were human food; water man's sole drink, they say. No bold hunters roamed the wood; none would then take life away — beasts and birds would sport and play with young children day by day. On this earth our sire then came, young and brave Wadili: he saw their maidens, felt love's flame, took them, fair, his wives to be, and taught the native arts you see — hunting, fishing, husbandry.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Origin of Living Creatures'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Origin of the White Race: Wood Cast Upon the Sea

region.zh: 圭亞那濱海阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part I 'Legends of the Arawaks', 'Origin of the White Race'

summary.en: Some addition has been made to that legend, grave and old, since our fathers surveyed steel-clad white men, strong and bold, who with blood-hounds, we are told, hunted men — and all for gold! 'Not from the Komaka tree sprang the whites,' our sages say: 'they, from wood cast on the sea, rose amidst wild ocean's spray, finding land on which to stay over the waters — far away.' 'If from wood our race has sprung, did it in these forests grow? Did it to green-heart belong, locust, or balata? Did its foliage ruddy glow with a mora's strength below? Ask no more, friend, you are wrong: those trees give us bark, gums, and timber strong — but the white man's stock, they say, good for nought, was cast away!' Smiles on every face appear; red men seated on the ground laugh to hear that satire old — a mild revenge which poor men found who escaped Spanish arcabuz and hound in the swamps around.
summary.zh: 自先祖見鋼甲白人以血犬獵人、專為掠金，古傳說遂增一篇。耆老言：『白人非自柯瑪卡樹出；乃擲海之木，起於怒濤之間，覓遠方之陸而居。』或問：『若吾族出自木，則此木生於此林乎？綠心木耶？洋槐耶？巴拉塔耶？』答曰：『毋多問，君誤矣。此諸樹日日賜我樹皮、樹膠、堅材；白人之材，無用而見棄者也！』紅人席地而笑——逃西班牙火銃與獵犬者之小復仇也。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880; a satire on the Spanish conquest embedded in the legend cycle, read critically.

passages.text: Some addition has been made to that legend, grave and old, since our fathers here surveyed steel-clad white men, strong and bold. They, with blood-hounds, we are told, hunted men — and all for gold! 'Not from the Komaka tree sprang the whites,' our sages say: 'they from wood cast on the sea rose amidst wild ocean's spray, finding land on which to stay over the waters — far away.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Origin of the White Race'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'If from wood our race has sprung, did it in these forests grow? Did it to green-heart belong, locust, or balata? Ask no more, friend, you are wrong. Those trees give us, day by day, bark, or gums, and timber strong: useful gifts they all convey. But the white man's stock, they say, good for nought, was cast away!' Smiles on every face appear; red men, seated on the ground, laugh that satire old to hear: a mild revenge, which poor men found who escaped, in swamps around, Spanish arcabuz and hound!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Origin of the White Race'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Fire: the First Destruction of the Arawak World
title.zh: 天火：阿拉瓦克世界之首滅

region.zh: 圭亞那濱海阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part I 'Legends of the Arawaks', 'The Fire and the Flood'

summary.en: The Arawaks, peculiar, understood that fire had swept the earth before the water-flood. Fire is mighty, all-subduing: once its fury came when the Maker, roused, was viewing deeds of blood and shame — evil raging, goodness failing — then on earth His wrath prevailing came the burning flame. Timely warning came from heaven: 'Fire shall sweep the land!' One who heard that warning sought a reef of sand and led his little band to dig a pit, hide wives and children under a strong timber roof, and to fell and burn all around until nothing on which flames could fasten remained. Clouds of smoke came rolling nigher, then fierce flames wrapped the woods in fire: the blazing torrent came onward, the burnt clearing stayed its current — there the flames expired. Thither, from that danger flying, birds and beasts repaired; and in their vault those men were lying, bearing smoke and heat while the fiery hail was pouring, finding safety there. Coming forth they saw the ruin through the lurid fume: blackened skeletons showed where men and beasts, when flying, met their awful doom.
summary.zh: 阿拉瓦克人獨知：洪水之前，先有天火。火威莫禦；造物主見人間血腥與醜惡，怒而生焰。天降警曰：『火將燎原！』一酋聞之，率眾至沙礁，鑿窖藏婦孺，以堅木覆之；又伐燒四周，使無可燃之物。煙雲漸近，烈焰裹林；火洪滾滾而至，遇焚清之地而止——焰乃熄。飛禽走獸亦奔集焉；窖中人忍煙受熱，得免於焚。出而視之：灰燼遍地，黑骸橫陳，皆奔逃者之終也。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded by Brett 1880 in metrical form; paraphrased into prose. Fire-before-flood destruction, read critically.

passages.text: Fire is mighty — all-subduing! Once its fury came, when the Maker, roused, was viewing deeds of blood and shame — evil raging, goodness failing — then on earth, His wrath prevailing, came the burning flame. Timely warning came from heaven: 'Fire shall sweep the land!' One who heard that warning given sought a reef of sand; by that chieftain's wisdom guided, some a refuge there provided for their little band.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Fire and the Flood'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Here,' said he, 'a pit preparing, wives and children hide; timber strong, the sand-roof bearing, we must first provide. Felling next the trees, and burning all around make clear; shrubs and grass to ashes turning, leave we nothing here — nothing on which flames can fasten. Clear and burn! O brothers! hasten, ere the flames appear!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Fire and the Flood'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Clouds of smoke, the sun concealing, came still rolling nigher; then fierce flames, their might revealing, wrapped the woods in fire. Onward came the blazing torrent: that burnt clearing stayed its current — there the flames expired. Thither, from that danger flying, birds and beasts repaired; in their vault those men were lying, smoke and heat they bore, while the flames around were roaring, and the fiery hail was pouring — finding safety there. Coming forth they saw the ruin through the lurid fume: blackened skeletons there lying showed where men and beasts, when flying, met their awful doom!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Fire and the Flood'; not verbatim.

title.en: Marerewana's Canoe and the Bush-Rope Mooring
title.zh: 馬雷瓦納之舟與藤索之繫

region.zh: 圭亞那濱海阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part I 'Legends of the Arawaks', 'The Fire and the Flood', part II

summary.en: Time flowed on; punishment became a stranger, and all had gone astray. When a new warning told them of a flood impending, none believed it true — till Marerewana, fearing for his wife and children, made a great canoe. Some of his neighbours said he was to blame; others, mocking at his labours, strove to give him shame: 'Make it large, Marerewana! Over forest and savannah float — the deluge through!' Still he worked, morning and evening, until the great waters came. An arched roof he thatched above it with strong warm palm leaves. 'When this flood shall come, we may drift, perhaps to-morrow, through the salt-sea foam!' he said with sorrow — and a voice answered: 'That great tree near thee: moor to that — thy craft shall bear thee safely near thy home!' Then, with lengthened bush-ropes mooring, he and his, the flood enduring, weathered surge and swell; and when the waters left them stranded, near their former home they landed — known, and loved, so well!
summary.zh: 時流而罰寢，眾皆放僻。洪水之警再至，無人信之——惟馬雷瓦納懼妻孥之亡，造巨舟。鄰人或咎之，或嘲之：『造大些，馬雷瓦納！漂過林野，浮出洪水！』彼朝夕勤作，不辭勞苦，直至大水至。舟上覆拱頂，以厚棕葉蔽之。彼憂曰：『洪水至時，吾儕恐漂入鹹海之沫。』有聲答曰：『近有大樹，繫舟其上——水退必近故里！』乃以長藤繫之；洪經而舟安，水退登岸，故里宛然在望。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded by Brett 1880; variant of the flood record already in the corpus, read critically.

passages.text: Time flowed on. That fearful danger long had passed away; punishment became a stranger; all had gone astray. Violence and wrong abounded; men with evil good confounded, growing worse each day. Evil ways have evil ending: when a warning new told them of a flood impending, none believed it true — till Marerewana, hearing, for his wife and children fearing, made a great canoe.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Fire and the Flood' II; not verbatim.

passages.text: Some among his nearest neighbours said he was to blame; others, mocking at his labours, strove to give him shame. Still they found him at it working, morn and eve, no labour shirking, ere 'great waters' came. 'Make it large, Marerewana! Strong and fair to view: over forest and savannah float — the deluge through!' Thus they mocked their anxious neighbour, laughed at his canoe. An arched roof he thatched above it, palm leaves strong and warm; firm, that no fierce wind might move it, ready for the storm.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Fire and the Flood' II; not verbatim.

passages.text: Still he feared, and said with sorrow: 'When this flood shall come, we may drift, perhaps to-morrow, through the salt-sea foam!' Said a voice: 'That great tree near thee, moor to that — thy craft shall bear thee safely near thy home!' Then, with lengthened bush-ropes mooring (so our legends tell), he and his, the flood enduring, weathered surge and swell. When the waters left them stranded, near their former home they landed — known, and loved, so well!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'The Fire and the Flood' II; not verbatim.

title.en: The Elder of Cuba and the Two Ways of the Soul
title.zh: 古巴老者與靈魂之兩路

texts.period: Taino tradition as told to Columbus; retold 1880 (Brett)

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part I 'Legends of the Arawaks', 'Ideas of a Future State'

summary.en: Columbus told how, on fair Cuba's isle, where, spent with toil, he sought repose awhile, and gentle natives welcomed him to land, a venerable elder took his hand. Full fourscore years had bowed that old man's head, and to the Admiral thus solemnly he said: 'Great is thy power, O chief! But be not vain, and from all violence and wrong abstain. For, after death, there are before the soul two ways, each ending in a final goal: to light and life all the kind-hearted go; the cruel and unkind to dark and dismal woe!'
summary.zh: 哥倫布述古巴島事：其倦而登陸，土人善遇之；一老者執其手——年已八十——肅然言曰：『酋長！權大勿驕，戒暴戒虐。人死之後，靈前有二路，各有終點：仁善者向光明與生；殘忍者向幽暗與苦！』

sensitivity.note: Taino tradition as retold through Columbus and Brett 1880; archival record, read critically.

passages.text: Columbus told how, on fair Cuba's isle, where, spent with toil, he sought repose awhile, and gentle natives welcomed him to land, a venerable elder took his hand. Full fourscore years had bowed that old man's head, and to the Admiral thus solemnly he said: 'Great is thy power, O chief! But be not vain, and from all violence and wrong abstain. For, after death, there are before the soul two ways, each ending in a final goal: to light and life all the kind-hearted go; the cruel and unkind to dark and dismal woe!'

title.en: Arawanili and the Orehu, the Lady of the Sea
title.zh: 阿拉瓦尼利與海母奧雷胡

region.zh: 安的列斯群島凱里島（阿拉瓦克）

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part I 'Legends of the Arawaks', 'Arawanili and the Orehu'

summary.en: A chieftain grave, both wise and brave — good Arawanili — stood mournful by the silver wave of the wide-spread ocean sea. His heart was sore: the plume he wore as chief of Kaieri drooped, while he listened on the shore to the sigh of that ocean sea. Throughout the isle man, wife, and child lay crushed by fever, driven wild by the demons' arrows — the dire shafts of the Yauhahu; and none without a charm could face them. Then in his view bright Orehu, the Water-Mother, rose glistening from the ocean sea: 'Go, plant with care this branch I bear, and rear the ida tree; when fruit is found, take that which first falls on the ground, and meet me by the sea!' He emptied the calabash's rind through holes; she brought its feathered handle, and, diving, brought the gems of ocean and stones of shining white; tobacco too, which none then knew, brought she; with charms which made all Yauhahu dread Arawanili. To her he owed the power he showed — none since like him could be. Still in stream or bay the Orehu men see; but 'high above', grown old, they say, rests Arawanili.
summary.zh: 智勇之酋阿拉瓦尼立於銀浪之濱而悲。凱里島中老幼為熱病所苦，為雅烏哈胡之毒箭所傷；無符者莫能當之。海母奧雷胡自波中出，曰：『植我所授之枝，育伊達樹；初落之果取而攜至海濱見我。』遂剖葫蘆為鈴，得羽柄；彼潛海而得白石；並授菸草——時人未知者也——與鎮雅烏哈胡之符。其能皆出於彼；至今無匹。今人猶於溪灣見奧雷胡；而阿拉瓦尼則老而高棲於天。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded by the missionary Brett 1880 in verse; paraphrased into prose and read critically.

passages.text: A chieftain grave, both wise and brave — good Arawanili — stood mournful by the silver wave of the wide-spread ocean sea. His heart was sore; the plume he wore as chief of Kaieri drooped, while he listened on the shore to the sigh of that ocean sea. 'Tis for the dead, the chieftain said, for whom I nought could do, to help them ere their spirits fled from torturing Yauhahu: throughout this isle, man, wife, or child, by fever crushed I view; by demons' arrows driven wild — dire shafts of Yauhahu! But none, without a charm, I trow, can face the Yauhahu.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Arawanili and the Orehu'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then, in his view, bright Orehu — the Water-Mother she — rose, glistening as with drops of dew, or pearls, from the ocean sea. 'Tell me thy grief, O chief! And I, perchance, may bring relief from the depths of the ocean sea. Go, plant with care this branch I bear, and rear the ida tree; when fruit is found, full large and round, take that which first falls on the ground, and meet me by the sea!'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Arawanili and the Orehu'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Its rind with care he emptied there through holes; she brought its handle, feathered fair; and while he wrought, she dived and sought the gems of ocean sea, and stones of shining white she brought. Tobacco too, which none then knew (though common now), brought she: with charms which made all Yauhahu dread Arawanili. To her he owed the power he showed — none since like him could be. Still, to this day, in stream or bay, the Orehu men see; but 'high above', grown old, they say, rests Arawanili.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Arawanili and the Orehu'; not verbatim.

title.en: Biter Bit: the Piai and the Sick White Man
title.zh: 反噬：巫醫與詐病之白人

region.zh: 圭亞那內地（阿拉瓦克巫俗）

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part I 'Legends of the Arawaks', 'Appendix to the Legend (Biter Bit)'

summary.en: Allusion was made to the tricks in their trade which Indian sorcerers have commonly played — here is what really happened a few years ago. Two white men went through the backwoods wishing to learn the piai mystery; one feigned sickness, and his friend begged the famous piai-man near by to come and cure 'this sick white man'. The sorcerer sternly bade the females take themselves away, made up his sacred fire to burn the sacred weed, commenced incantations terrible to hear, inhaled tobacco smoke and blew it over and up the sick man's nose, rubbed the affected part till the patient shook with stifled laughter he could hold out no more — then, according to their ancient rules, applied his mouth to suck out what was causing the pain, gripping with his teeth full sore until, with a yell, the patient fell out on the earthen floor. The cool doctor by signs made his meaning plain: 'Get back into that hammock; I must operate again!' — and the white man, cash and fame secure, walked off triumphantly, having told him he had made a cure and given a handsome fee. And when a man is learning the mysteries of his vocation, he is shut up and half-starved, drinks tobacco decoction as strong as can be, till he sinks in a trance — and revives an M.D.!
summary.zh: 巫醫行技之詭，姑舉一實事。二白人入林欲學巫秘；一人詐病，友人請近地名巫醫來治。巫驅婦人，焚聖草，誦咒震耳，吸菸而吹病者鼻中，搓其痛處；病者忍癢不禁，笑聲大作——巫面不改色。依古法以口吸其痛處，齧之極痛；病者呼而仆地。巫以手示意：『回床！吾須再施術！』白人自知技窮，乃賞金而稱其治愈，揚長而去。至若學巫之人：閉戶半饑，飲至濃之菸汁，昏眩而醒——即成醫師矣！

sensitivity.note: Arawak piai practice described by the missionary Brett 1880; a colonial-era anecdote about shamanic curing technique, read critically — it records real ritual procedure (tobacco fumigation, sucking extraction) alongside colonial mockery.

passages.text: Two white men through our backwoods went, the Indian life to see, and much they wished of piai-men to learn the mystery. But 'twas in vain, till one declared that he was 'taken sick', and begged his friend to lend a hand to carry out the trick. They knew a famous piai-man lived at a place near by: 'Oh come and cure this sick white man!' He answered: 'I will try.' He first the females sternly bade to take themselves away; they all forthwith fled like the wind, too much afraid to stay. He then made up his sacred fire to burn the sacred weed; his incantations then commenced, most terrible to hear.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Appendix to the Legend'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He next inhaled tobacco smoke, much as his mouth could hold, and blew it on the sick white man. He next on the affected part his hands began to rub; the patient grew convulsed at that — with strong but stifled laughter his body shook all over: he could hold out no more! He laughed outright, then feebly tried to make that laugh a groan: the doctor knew the difference of tone, saw that he was being tricked, yet went on with his work, not altering a muscle, but as grave as any Turk.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Appendix to the Legend'; not verbatim.

passages.text: According to their ancient rules, his mouth he next applied to suck out what was causing pain in that white man's inside; he seized him boldly with his teeth — it was a grip full sore — and, with a yell, the patient fell out on the earthen floor! Most cool the doctor was: by signs he made his meaning plain: 'Get back into that hammock, I must operate again!' The other shook his head, showed his injured side, and said 'twas bitten through — but he replied: 'This savage doctor knows a thing or two; I'll tell him he has made a cure, and give a handsome fee.' So he, with cash and fame secure, walked off triumphantly. When a man's on probation, learning the mysteries of his vocation, he's shut up and half-starved; drinks tobacco decoction as strong as can be, till he sinks in a trance: and revives — an M.D.!
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Brett 1880, 'Appendix to the Legend'; not verbatim.

title.en: Arawidi the Sun and the Woodpecker Watchman
title.zh: 太陽阿拉威迪與啄木守望

region.zh: 圭亞那濱海阿拉瓦克之地

source.work: W. H. Brett, Legends and Myths of the Aboriginal Indians of British Guiana (1880), Part I 'Legends of the Arawaks', 'Arawidi (A Fragment)'

summary.en: 'Adaili is the glorious sun' — thus their first legend ran — 'but when of old on earth he came, then Arawidi was his name: his fashion, that of man.' Once, fishing on a favourite stream, he made a dam or weir, and said: 'This stream must not run dry, lest, in my visits from the sky, I find no fishes here.' The otters heard; they broke his dam and let the waters flow. Then he, compelled to seek for aid, made the woodpecker his watchman here below. One day, while passing through the sky, loud tapping caught his ear: swift darting to that spot below he found a fierce and mailed foe — the alligator — near. He seized him with a mighty hand, and smote to make the reptile yield with his war club upon his head and tail. 'Oh, Arawidi, slay me not!' the alligator cried: 'Cease to wound! Thy suppliant spare, and I will give a maiden fair to be thy beauteous bride.' He called his friends the water-sprites, the maiden to provide; and soon a girl of wondrous charms was placed in Arawidi's arms. The reptile's wounds were healed, but still their marks are seen, 'tis said, indented on his battered head and notched along his tail.
summary.zh: 『阿達利即榮耀之日』——其首傳如此——『古時降凡，名阿拉威迪，形貌如人。』彼於慣釣之溪築堰，曰：『此水毋涸，免我自天再臨時無魚。』水獺聞而毀堰；彼遂以啄木鳥為守望。一日自天過，聞叩聲甚急；俯臨其地，見鱷——披甲之勁敵也。執之以巨手，以戰杖擊其首尾。鱷呼曰：『阿拉威迪，毋殺我！饒我，當獻美女為爾妻。』遂召水靈獻女；美人入懷。鱷創雖愈，而其首之凹痕、尾之齒痕，至今猶見。

sensitivity.note: Arawak oral tradition recorded by Brett 1880 in verse; paraphrased into prose. Variant of the Roth Arawidi record.

Once, fishing on a fav'rite stream, he made a dam, or weir, and said: This stream must not run dry, lest, in my visits from the sky, I find no fishes here. The otters heard.
